You are a research group coordinator who needs to document analysis of three foundational papers in language model research. Your task is to analyze three specific papers available in the paper database, create structured notes in your team's Notion workspace, and compile a formal Word report.

The three papers you need to analyze are: "Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models" (arXiv ID 2301.07041), "Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback" (arXiv ID 2203.11171), and "OPT: Open Pre-trained Transformer Language Models" (arXiv ID 2205.01068). Use the arXiv and LaTeX analysis tools to retrieve full text and analyze each paper's structure, sections, and key contributions.

For each paper, create a Notion page in your workspace with the paper title as the page title, prefixed with "Paper: ". Include structured notes in the page body covering the paper's main contributions, methodology, and key findings based on the full text you retrieve.

Create a Word document called Paper_Analysis_Report.docx in your workspace. The document should start with a title "Comparative Paper Analysis Report" and include a section for each of the three papers. Each section heading should identify the paper clearly. Within each section, describe the paper's title, key contributions, and methodology. After the three individual sections, include a final section titled "Comparative Analysis" that draws connections between the three papers, discussing how they relate to each other in terms of their contributions to large language model research.

Send an email to research_lead@university.edu with subject "Paper Analysis Report Ready" summarizing what you have done and noting that the Word document and Notion pages are ready for review.

Task-Solving Rationable with Sub-task Decomposition:
To solve this task efficiently,

The three fixed-paper source stage is small enough for the main agent; use sub-agents only for the two independent output owners. All research is read-only.

Resolve the task-visible workspace directory from the runtime allowed-directory listing (or the literal accessible-workspace directory already supplied by the harness), freeze it as `<workspace_root>`, and reject bare `/workspace` and dumps/run-specific paths. Freeze the three task-specified ID/title slots: `2301.07041 / Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models`, `2203.11171 / Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback`, and `2205.01068 / OPT: Open Pre-trained Transformer Language Models`.

Issue the arXiv record and arxiv-latex section calls for all three IDs in one native-parallel source response. Verify each returned stable ID/title even if the task's pairing is unusual; do not silently replace a task slot from outside knowledge. For each slot extract title, complete authors when returned, contributions, methodology, findings, section list/count, provenance, and missing/conflict status. Reconcile once and freeze one literal canonical three-paper packet; the Notion pages, Word report, and email consume this exact packet without re-researching or recomputing claims.

1. Wave 1 — dispatch exactly 2 coder sub-agents in parallel as individual Agent calls:

   1. coder 0 (external-workflow-operator 0): Notion owner: search exact titles `Paper: <canonical title>`; reuse one exact match, create at most one page on zero matches, and block on duplicates. Own all three pages in one agent so parent IDs and idempotency stay consistent. Each page must contain substantive Contribution, Methodology, and Findings blocks copied from the canonical packet. Read all three pages back and return IDs, exact titles, stable-ID coverage, and block validation. Do not write the Word file or email.
   2. coder 1 (office-report-builder 0): Word owner: create `<workspace_root>/Paper_Analysis_Report.docx` exactly once, preferably atomically with `python-docx`, with the required report title, one clearly headed section per canonical paper, and a final Comparative Analysis grounded only in those records. Read it back and return path, heading order, exact paper/title coverage, and validation. Do not modify Notion or email.

In the same response that launches Wave 1, the main agent paginates Sent search for exact To `research_lead@university.edu` and Subject `Paper Analysis Report Ready`, reading every candidate. After both outputs return, send exactly once only if no exact match exists, mentioning the verified Word filename and the three verified Notion page titles/IDs. Never retry an ambiguous send. Accept only after all pages, the document, and exactly one message read back against the canonical packet.

=== PAGE 1 ===
Title: "Paper: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models"
Overview: arXiv: 2301.07041 — Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, Tom Henighan, et al. A foundational empirical study showing that language model performance improves predictably as a power law in model size, dataset size, and training compute.
Main Contributions (bullets):
- Establishes empirical scaling laws for language model performance (cross-entropy loss) as power laws in model size, dataset size, and training compute.
- Demonstrates the power-law trends hold over more than seven orders of magnitude, making performance predictable far beyond the scales at which models are actually trained.
- Shows that architectural details (network width or depth) have minimal effects on performance within a wide range — scale matters, not shape.
- Derives simple equations governing overfitting as a function of model/dataset size, and training speed as a function of model size.
- Provides a framework for optimally allocating a fixed compute budget between model size and data size.
Methodology: The paper is a large-scale empirical measurement study of Transformer language model training. The authors trained a fleet of over 1,000 language models spanning three orders of magnitude in scale, and fit cross-entropy validation loss against the three principal scaling axes: number of parameters N, dataset size D (in tokens), and training compute C. The core device is fitting power laws of the form L(N) = (Nc/N)^αN (with analogues for D and C), estimating the exponents from observed loss trajectories across the model fleet. Beyond the one-dimensional fits, they analyze how the joint dependence of loss on N and D governs overfitting, how training speed varies with model size, and how the fitted laws prescribe the optimal split of a fixed compute budget between larger models and more data.
Key Findings (bullets):
- Loss follows power laws in all three axes, with exponents approximately α_N ≈ 0.076 (model size), α_D ≈ 0.095 (dataset size), and α_C ≈ 0.050 (training compute).
- Some scaling trends span more than seven orders of magnitude, an extraordinary range of validity.
- Architecture is nearly irrelevant within a wide range: width/depth have minimal effect; overall scale governs loss.
- Larger models are more sample-efficient, reaching a given loss level faster than smaller models.
- The laws were validated by training over 1,000 models spanning three orders of magnitude, enabling forecasting of large-model performance from small-scale experiments and optimal compute-budget allocation.
Relation to LLM Research: This is the foundational empirical study behind the modern "scale-first" paradigm: it showed that LLM loss is a smooth, predictable function of parameters, data, and compute rather than of architectural minutiae. That predictability lets labs forecast huge models from cheap small-scale runs and allocate compute optimally, directly informing GPT-3-scale designs and seeding the follow-up literature on compute-optimal (Chinchilla-style) scaling, data-constrained scaling, and scaling-law-based model selection.

=== PAGE 2 ===
Title: "Paper: Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback"
Overview: arXiv: 2203.11171 — Long Ouyang, Jeff Wu, Xu Jiang, et al. (the InstructGPT paper). Aligns GPT-3 to follow user instructions using reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF).
Main Contributions (bullets):
- Introduces InstructGPT: language models starting from GPT-3 that are trained to follow user instructions, using RLHF to align model outputs with human intent.
- Presents a three-step alignment pipeline: (1) supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on human demonstration data, (2) training a reward model from human preference comparisons, and (3) fine-tuning with PPO using the reward model.
- Shows that a much smaller aligned model (1.3B parameters) is preferred by human labelers over the far larger base GPT-3 (175B parameters) — alignment training, not scale alone, drives helpfulness.
- Demonstrates that RLHF improves truthfulness (measured on TruthfulQA) and reduces toxicity relative to the base model.
- Shows these alignment gains come with minimal trade-off in general capabilities.
Methodology: The work starts from GPT-3 and aligns it to user intent via a three-stage procedure. Step 1: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on demonstration data written by humans, giving the model initial instruction-conditioned behavior. Step 2: a reward model is trained from human preference comparisons — labelers compare candidate model outputs and the reward model learns to score outputs in a way that predicts these preferences. Step 3: the SFT model is fine-tuned with PPO (proximal policy optimization), using the reward model as the reward signal. Evaluation is human-preference-based (labelers compare InstructGPT outputs against GPT-3 outputs), supplemented by TruthfulQA for truthfulness and toxicity measurement; the key contrast is the aligned 1.3B InstructGPT against the 175B GPT-3.
Key Findings (bullets):
- InstructGPT (1.3B parameters) is preferred by human evaluators over GPT-3 (175B parameters) on 85% of prompts, despite being roughly 100x smaller.
- RLHF-trained models are more truthful, with improved performance on TruthfulQA relative to base GPT-3.
- RLHF-trained models are less toxic than the base model.
- The SFT → reward model → PPO pipeline yields substantial improvements in following user instructions.
- These gains come with minimal trade-off in general capabilities.
Relation to LLM Research: This is the foundational alignment paper for modern instruction-tuned LLMs: it established the now-standard SFT → reward modeling → RLHF pipeline underlying instruction-following assistants and directly prefigured ChatGPT-style systems. Its central result — a 1.3B RLHF model outperforming 175B base GPT-3 in human preference — reframed LLM progress from pure scale toward alignment with human intent, and popularized TruthfulQA and toxicity as standard alignment evaluation axes.

=== PAGE 3 ===
Title: "Paper: OPT: Open Pre-trained Transformer Language Models"
Overview: arXiv: 2205.01068 — Meta AI. Releases OPT, a fully open-source family of decoder-only Transformer language models spanning 125M to 175B parameters.
Main Contributions (bullets):
- Release of OPT, a suite of fully open-source large language models spanning parameter sizes from 125M to 175B.
- Demonstration that open models can match the closed frontier: OPT models match or exceed GPT-3 on most NLP benchmarks while being completely open.
- Full transparency of the training process: documentation of the training methodology, hardware infrastructure, and lessons learned from training at scale.
- Public release of model weights and training code, enabling the research community to study large language models previously restricted to closed, proprietary models.
Methodology: OPT is a family of decoder-style language models built on the standard Transformer architecture, configured with pre-norm layer normalization, ReLU activations, and learned positional embeddings, and trained with the AdamW optimizer. The training corpus combines Common Crawl, Wikipedia, and other datasets totaling roughly 800 GB. Training at the 175B scale was made feasible through a distributed infrastructure using tensor and pipeline model parallelism across up to 992 A100 GPUs, and the paper documents this hardware setup and the operational lessons learned from large-scale training. Evaluation uses standard zero-shot and few-shot NLP benchmarks, with the flagship OPT-175B compared against GPT-3; weights plus training code are released openly.
Key Findings (bullets):
- The OPT suite spans 125M to 175B parameters, with OPT-175B as the flagship model.
- OPT-175B matches or exceeds GPT-3 on most zero-shot and few-shot NLP benchmarks.
- Training data totaled approximately 800 GB (Common Crawl, Wikipedia, and other datasets).
- Training was distributed via tensor and pipeline parallelism across up to 992 A100 GPUs.
- The architecture/optimizer configuration (pre-norm, ReLU, learned positional embeddings, AdamW) was deliberately kept close to standard practice for reproducibility.
- Full model weights and training code were released publicly.
Relation to LLM Research: A landmark in the democratization of large language models: before OPT, the strongest ~175B-scale models (like GPT-3) were closed, and OPT provided the first openly available suite of comparable quality, enabling reproduction, ablation, and study of scaling behavior by the broader community. Its documented training recipe and parallelism strategy established a practical reference for engineering LLMs and paved the way for the wave of open-source LLMs that followed.

Read in order of publication — scaling laws, instruction tuning, and open pre-training — they describe a coherent research program: first establish how capability scales, then make that capability useful and safe, then make it accessible to everyone."
- "Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models provides the quantitative foundation. By showing that loss falls as a smooth power law in parameters, data, and compute — largely independent of architectural details — it justified the massive compute budgets behind models like GPT-3 and made it possible to forecast frontier performance from small-scale experiments. Both InstructGPT and OPT build directly on this world: InstructGPT begins from GPT-3, a model whose very scale was justified by scaling-law reasoning, while OPT replicates a GPT-3-class training run (125M–175B parameters, ~800 GB of data, up to 992 A100 GPUs) openly, empirically confirming that the scaling recipe is reproducible outside a closed lab."
- "InstructGPT adds the crucial corrective that scale alone does not equal usefulness: its 1.3B-parameter RLHF-tuned model was preferred by human evaluators over the 175B-parameter base GPT-3 on 85% of prompts. (OPT) answer how to build and share such models openly. All three rest on the same decoder-only Transformer backbone, underscoring the scaling-laws finding that architecture matters far less than scale, alignment, and accessibility."
